topics.title: Matter is made of tiny particles

learn.hook: Light an agarbatti in one corner of the room and soon the whole room smells of it. The smell travels without anyone carrying it. How?
points: All matter is made of extremely tiny particles, far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope.
There are spaces between particles. When sugar dissolves in water, its particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
Particles are always moving. When particles of one substance spread out and mix with another by themselves, it is called diffusion.
Diffusion is faster when the temperature is higher, because heated particles move faster. Diffusion is fastest in gases and slowest in solids.
Particles attract each other. This force of attraction holds them together; it is strongest in solids and weakest in gases.

example.q: Think it through: A drop of ink is gently added to a glass of hot water and another to a glass of cold water. In which glass does the colour spread through faster, and why?
steps: The colour spreads because ink particles and water particles keep moving and mixing: diffusion.
Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster.
example.answer: In the hot water, because its particles move faster and diffusion happens more quickly.

learn.reallife: You can tell someone is frying pakoras in the kitchen from your room. The smell particles diffuse through the air, and hot food's smell spreads quickly.

games.title: Particle facts
items: All matter is made of tiny particles.
This is the basic idea of the particulate nature of matter.
There are no spaces between particles of a liquid.
There are spaces; that is how sugar or salt can dissolve in water.
Particles of matter are always moving.
Even in a solid, particles keep vibrating.
Diffusion is faster in hot water than in cold water.
Heated particles move faster, so they mix sooner.
Diffusion is fastest in solids.
Diffusion is fastest in gases, where particles move most freely.

games.title: Spread speed
items: A solid placed against another solid
Ink in cold water
Ink in hot water
Perfume smell in air

quiz.q: Why does the smell of a burning agarbatti fill a room?
options: Scent particles diffuse through the air
quiz.explain: Particles of the scent move about and mix with air particles, spreading through the room by diffusion.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the spreading of smell with moving particles

quiz.q: Sugar dissolves in a glass of water and the water level barely rises. What does this show?
options: There are spaces between water particles
Water particles are bigger than glass
quiz.explain: Sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles, so the volume barely changes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dissolved sugar is destroyed

quiz.q: In which does diffusion happen fastest?
quiz.explain: Gas particles are far apart and move very fast, so they mix quickly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks closely packed particles mix fastest

quiz.q: What effect does heating have on the particles of a substance?
quiz.explain: Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster. The particles themselves do not grow.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heating makes particles themselves grow larger

quiz.q: What holds the particles of a solid together?
quiz.explain: Particles attract each other, and this attraction is strongest in solids.
quiz.mistake: Does not know about interparticle attraction

quiz.q: A crystal dissolved in water colours a whole jug, and even after dilution the water stays a little coloured. What does this tell us?
options: Each crystal contains a huge number of very tiny particles
The crystal is made of one big particle
quiz.explain: The colour spreads through a big volume because the crystal breaks into countless tiny particles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a crystal is one solid piece with no particles

quiz.q: The spreading of particles of one substance among another on their own is called:
quiz.explain: Diffusion happens because particles keep moving and mixing by themselves.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up scientific terms

quiz.q: Why can we smell hot food from far away more easily than cold food?
options: Hot food particles move faster and diffuse quickly
Cold food has no smell at all
quiz.explain: Heat makes particles move faster, so the smell reaches us sooner.
quiz.mistake: Does not link temperature with the speed of diffusion

teach.ask: Gappu sniffs: How does the smell of jalebis reach me from the shop across the street? Nobody brought it here!
teach.praise: Smell particles keep moving and spread through the air by diffusion, right into my beak. Yum!
teach.nudge: What is the smell made of? And what are those things always doing?

topics.title: Solids, liquids, gases and the spaces between particles

learn.hook: Why can a lot of CNG be squeezed into the small cylinder of an auto-rickshaw, but you cannot squeeze a brick even a little?
points: Solids: particles are very closely packed with very little space between them and strong attraction. They only vibrate in place, so solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume.
Liquids: particles are a little farther apart with weaker attraction. They can slide past each other, so liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container.
Gases: particles are far apart with very weak attraction and move freely in all directions. Gases have no fixed shape or volume and fill any container.
Because gas particles have large spaces between them, gases can be compressed a lot. Solids and liquids can hardly be compressed.
Changing the state of a substance (like ice to water) changes the arrangement and spacing of its particles, not the particles themselves.

example.q: Think it through: You press the plunger of a sealed syringe filled with air, then one filled with water. What happens and why? (Do not point a syringe at anyone.)
steps: Air particles have large spaces between them.
Pressing pushes air particles closer, so the plunger moves in a lot.
Water particles are already close together, so the plunger hardly moves.
example.answer: The air syringe compresses easily but the water syringe hardly at all, because gas particles have much more space between them.

learn.reallife: CNG for autos and buses and oxygen for hospitals are stored in compressed form in strong cylinders, possible only because gases can be squeezed.

games.title: Everyday matter
pairs: Coconut oil on a warm day

quiz.q: In which state are particles packed most closely?
quiz.explain: Solid particles are tightly packed with very little space between them.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how particle spacing differs across states

quiz.q: Why does milk take the shape of the glass it is poured into?
options: Its particles can slide past each other
Its particles are fixed in place
Its particles are far apart like a gas
quiz.explain: Liquid particles can move past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the container's shape.
quiz.mistake: Thinks liquids have fixed positions like solids

quiz.q: Which can be compressed the most?
quiz.explain: Air is a gas with large spaces between particles, so pushing them closer is easy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks liquids compress as easily as gases

quiz.q: Which statement about gases is correct?
options: They fill the whole of any container
quiz.explain: Gas particles move freely in all directions and spread out to fill the container.
quiz.mistake: Applies properties of solids to gases

quiz.q: The force of attraction between particles is weakest in:
options: It is the same in all
quiz.explain: Gas particles are so far apart that the attraction between them is very weak.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of attraction strength

quiz.q: A liquid has:
options: Fixed volume but no fixed shape
Fixed shape but no fixed volume
Neither fixed shape nor fixed volume
quiz.explain: A litre of water stays a litre, but it takes the shape of a bottle or a bucket.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the properties of liquids and gases

quiz.q: When ice melts into water, what changes?
options: The arrangement and spacing of the same particles
quiz.explain: The water particles stay the same; only how they are arranged and how freely they move changes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a change of state makes new particles

quiz.q: Why do particles in a solid not move around freely?
options: Strong attraction holds them close in fixed positions
They have no energy at all
quiz.explain: Strong attraction keeps solid particles in place, though they still vibrate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks solid particles are completely still

teach.ask: Gappu pokes a stone, splashes water and flaps at the air: Why are these three so different if they are all made of particles?
teach.praise: Solid particles are packed close, liquid particles slide, and gas particles are far apart with big spaces. Same particles, different spacing!
teach.nudge: How close are the particles in each one? And how freely can they move?

learn.hook: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool on a hot summer day, even without a fridge?
points: Heating gives particles energy. At the melting point a solid turns into a liquid; ice melts at 0 °C.
At the boiling point a liquid turns into a gas throughout its volume. Pure water boils at 100 °C at sea level.
Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface, at temperatures below boiling. It is faster when it is hot, windy, dry, and when the surface area is larger.
Evaporation causes cooling: the faster-moving particles escape and take energy away. Sweating and the clay matka both cool this way.
Condensation is gas turning into liquid, as on the outside of a cold glass. Some solids, like camphor and naphthalene balls, change directly into vapour; this is sublimation.

example.q: Think it through: Clothes dry faster on a sunny, windy day than on a humid, still day. Why?
steps: Drying of clothes is evaporation of water.
Sunshine heats the water particles, so more escape.
Wind carries away the vapour, and dry air can take in more vapour than humid air.
example.answer: Heat, wind and dry air all speed up evaporation.

learn.reallife: Drops forming on the outside of a cold glass of nimbu pani are not leaking; they are water vapour from the air condensing on the cold surface.

games.title: Name the change
pairs: Water turning into ice in the freezer

items.text: Pure water boils at ___ °C at sea level.

quiz.q: At what temperature, in °C, does pure ice melt?
quiz.explain: Ice melts at 0 °C. Water freezes at the same temperature.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the melting point with the boiling point

quiz.q: At what temperature, in °C, does pure water boil at sea level?
quiz.explain: At normal sea-level pressure, pure water boils at 100 °C.
quiz.mistake: Does not remember the boiling point of water

quiz.q: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool?
options: Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates, causing cooling
quiz.explain: Evaporation from the outer surface takes heat away from the water inside.
quiz.mistake: Does not know evaporation causes cooling

quiz.q: Which condition makes wet clothes dry fastest?
quiz.explain: Heat and wind both speed up evaporation.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the factors affecting evaporation

quiz.q: Water drops on the outside of a cold glass come from:
options: Water vapour in the air condensing
quiz.explain: Air contains water vapour, which cools on the cold glass and turns into liquid drops.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the drops leak through the glass

quiz.q: Camphor kept open slowly disappears without turning into a liquid. This is:
quiz.explain: Sublimation is a solid changing directly into vapour.
quiz.mistake: Thinks everything must melt before becoming a gas

quiz.q: How is evaporation different from boiling?
options: Evaporation happens only from the surface and below the boiling point
Boiling happens only from the surface
quiz.explain: Evaporation goes on at any temperature from the surface; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks evaporation and boiling are the same

quiz.q: Why do we feel cool when sweat dries on our skin?
options: Evaporating sweat takes away heat from the skin
quiz.explain: The escaping water particles carry energy away, cooling the body.
quiz.mistake: Does not link evaporation with cooling

teach.ask: Gappu fans himself: Why does my water bowl get emptier on hot days even though I did not drink it?
teach.praise: The Sun's heat makes water particles at the surface escape into the air as vapour. That is evaporation!
teach.nudge: Where did the water go? What does heat do to the water particles at the top?
